title: How A Bill Becomes A Law

jokes.text: Is that a picture of you? Yes. I am big enough to admit that I am often inspired by myself.
jokes.setup: Leslie is showing Ben her wall of inspirational women.
jokes.punchline: One of the inspirational women is Leslie herself, and she owns it completely without shame.
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Leslie Knope — her self-confidence borders on grandiosity but is always played with sincerity rather than arrogance. The phrasing 'big enough to admit' is a perfect inversion: usually that phrase precedes a humble admission, but Leslie uses it to confess narcissism. High character integration because no other character on any show would deliver this line with this specific earnest conviction. Earns an 8 because it's compact, perfectly constructed, and deepens our understanding of Leslie in one beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is my wall of inspirational women. And this one right here... that's me.

jokes.text: Here are my clocks. Pawnee and Washington D.C. Same time zone.
jokes.setup: Leslie excitedly shows off her new office perks, including a two-clock setup implying important international or cross-timezone connections.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that both cities are in the same time zone — making the two-clock display entirely pointless — delivered with total pride.
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical joke — the punchline is embedded entirely in the setup with zero wasted words. Leslie's complete lack of self-awareness about the absurdity is what makes it land. The joke trusts the audience to do the math, which is a sign of confident writing. Very high economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And this is my private bathroom. No one else in the office has one of these.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, someone's in there.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, that's impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Sorry! I'll be out in a minute!

jokes.text: Councilman Jamm emerges from Leslie's private bathroom — 'Occupied!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is excitedly showing Ben her private bathroom, a coveted perk of her new office.
jokes.punchline: A stranger's voice yells 'Occupied!' from inside — her private bathroom is already being used by another councilman.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured comedic reveal. The buildup of Leslie's excitement about the bathroom is paid off immediately and unexpectedly by an interloper. The word 'Occupied!' is perfectly chosen — it's a word you only yell in a shared space, which immediately undercuts Leslie's sense of ownership. Strong structure and economy; lower character integration since it's a situational gag rather than character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I'm using Leslie's bathroom because the men's room was occupied. But I have to say, her bathroom is nicer. It's got better lighting, softer toilet paper, and these nice little soaps shaped like seashells.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, those are just normal bathroom amenities.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Exactly. Which is why women's bathrooms are superior. I mean, it only makes sense—women are better at decorating and paying attention to detail. It's just biology.

jokes.text: I think it is crazy that the most junior city councilor gets a private bathroom just because she is a girl.
jokes.setup: Councilman Jamm is explaining why he feels entitled to use Leslie's bathroom.
jokes.punchline: His justification reveals a casually sexist worldview, played as if it's a perfectly reasonable position.
jokes.explanation: Efficient villain-establishing joke. Jamm's casual sexism is played deadpan which makes it land as cringe comedy rather than pure offense. It establishes his character quickly and credibly as an antagonist while getting a laugh. Not highly original but well-executed for what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I propose we install a shared bathroom schedule. I use it Monday, Wednesday, Friday from 6 to 7 AM for my morning routine.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I sit on the toilet for approximately 23 minutes. I produce a substantial amount of waste. Sometimes it's diarrhea, sometimes it's more solid. On Wednesdays it's usually both.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I then spend 12 minutes wiping. I use roughly half a roll of toilet paper per session. I have very poor aim.

jokes.text: Tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to drop my liquids in here, take my solids down the hall. Deal?
jokes.setup: Jamm is trying to negotiate shared bathroom usage with Leslie.
jokes.punchline: He offers an extremely specific and degrading bathroom timeshare using clinical/crude terms, delivered as if he's offering a perfectly reasonable compromise.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'liquids' vs 'solids' is what elevates this above a generic crude joke. Jamm treats it like a formal negotiation, which maximizes the cringe. High character integration — this kind of boundary-free oversharing is core to the Jamm character. 'Drop my liquids' is also a slightly unusual phrase that adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?!

jokes.text: Leslie's horrified 'How?' reaction beat after Jamm leaves — implying he used her bathroom without flushing or cleaning up.
jokes.setup: Jamm leaves after the bathroom negotiation.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's single-word 'How?' implies she has discovered a bathroom disaster, played entirely through her reaction.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — the entire joke is a single word. The audience fills in all the gross details themselves, which is smarter than spelling it out. Strong structural choice to leave the bathroom aftermath to the imagination. Rewatch bonus because what she discovers is never shown, letting each viewer construct their own horror.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: My therapist said I should be more open and honest about my feelings. So I told a guy at the gym that his workout routine was making me uncomfortable because it made me feel inadequate about my own fitness level.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: He said, 'Thanks for sharing, man,' and then he moved to a different machine. My therapist said that's a win.

jokes.text: Fun fact about me. I recently began intensive psychotherapy. I may have mentioned that to you already. Several times.
jokes.setup: Chris introduces the topic of his therapy as a 'fun fact.'
jokes.punchline: His colleagues confirm he has mentioned it many, many times, while he remains oblivious to his own oversharing.
jokes.explanation: Calling his therapy oversharing a 'fun fact' is perfect character work — Chris's relentless positivity reframes everything as an exciting announcement. The 'several times' confirmation from colleagues grounds it in social reality while he remains blissfully unaware. Strong character integration for Chris Traeger's specific brand of earnest narcissism.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: We've been going to couples therapy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. I don't need to hear about your personal stuff, man. That's what therapy is for.

jokes.text: Well, like my therapist says, 'You can't share too much or too often.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just been told he's mentioned his therapy many times.
jokes.punchline: He justifies the oversharing by citing his therapist — who apparently told him the one piece of advice most likely to make him insufferable.
jokes.explanation: Works because the therapist's advice is plausibly well-intentioned but Chris applies it with zero social filter. The joke critiques therapy culture gently without being mean-spirited, which fits the show's warm tone. The irony that therapy is making Chris more annoying rather than better-adjusted is the core of his Season 5 arc.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: So I've been thinking about implementing a 311 system here in Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh man, that's a great idea!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Thank you, Andy. I'm glad you agree with me.

jokes.text: You know, Gayle and I, we saw a couples therapist for a little while. That's too much, Jerry. For real. Keep us out your bedroom.
jokes.setup: The group is discussing Chris's therapy. Jerry volunteers a personal anecdote about couples therapy.
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately shuts him down with 'That's too much, Jerry' — the classic Jerry dismissal, implying his oversharing is uniquely unwelcome.
jokes.explanation: Efficient use of the Jerry-as-butt-of-joke running gag. The irony is rich: Chris has been oversharing about therapy for the whole scene, but when Jerry does it once, he's immediately told to stop. Slightly formulaic Jerry gag but well-placed in context.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

jokes.text: Thank you, Andy. I agree. I love this idea. And I love me for thinking of it. My therapist said that I need to be more vocal about appreciating myself. Thank you, Chris. You're welcome, Chris. I sound insane. I'm going to go talk to my therapist.
jokes.setup: Chris thanks Andy for supporting his 311 idea, then segues into self-appreciation.
jokes.punchline: The sequence escalates from earnest self-praise into Chris having a full conversation with himself, culminating in his own self-aware 'I sound insane' before announcing he'll go see his therapist — completing the loop.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout Chris joke of the episode. The escalation is perfectly structured: self-praise → full self-dialogue → momentary self-awareness → immediately outsourcing that self-awareness to the therapist. The loop structure (therapy creates the problem; therapy is the solution) is elegant. 'I sound insane. I'm going to go talk to my therapist' is a highly quotable couplet. Strong 8 because it earns every beat through character logic and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I know how this sounds, but I think I need more therapy.

jokes.text: Pawnee's City Council approval rate is at a dismal 3%. That's an all-time low. Yuck.
jokes.setup: Joan is opening a news segment with statistics about the city council.
jokes.punchline: The journalistic gravitas of '3% approval' is immediately undercut by the extremely unprofessional editorial 'Yuck.'
jokes.explanation: Joan Callamezzo's character is defined by the gap between her self-important 'first-rate newswoman' persona and her actual unprofessionalism. 'Yuck' as an editorial opinion on a news broadcast perfectly captures this. Economy is high — the gap between formal statistic and childish reaction word does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's just your opinion.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Well, that's just your opinion.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, an opinion is a belief or judgment that rests on grounds insufficient to produce complete certainty. That's the definition.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: That's just your opinion.

jokes.text: No, that's your opinion. That's the definition of an opinion. Well, that's your opinion.
jokes.setup: Joan says something is 'a fact,' Leslie correctly identifies it as an opinion, Joan agrees — then immediately applies the word 'opinion' incorrectly back at Leslie.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, that's your opinion' — used to dismiss Leslie's accurate definition of the word 'opinion,' creating an absurd logical loop.
jokes.explanation: Tight logical construction — the joke works on a philosophical level (if 'that's your opinion' can be applied to anything, it means nothing) and a character level (Joan's intellectual laziness is perfectly captured). The three-line exchange is a model of economy: setup, definition, absurd inversion. Quotable because the structure can be lifted out of context and still makes sense as a joke about epistemology and bad-faith argument. Justifies its 8+ score by being both clever and efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to help the swim team because I believe in their cause. Plus, with a mascot like the Dolphins, how could I resist? They really have a porpoise!

jokes.text: I'm a city councilor with porpoise.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining why she took on the swimming bill, saying she's not just a city councilor.
jokes.punchline: 'With porpoise' — a pun on 'purpose,' tied to the Pawnee Porpoises swim team. Delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-constructed pun that only works because the episode has organically set up the Pawnee Porpoises context. The joke doesn't announce itself — Leslie delivers it as if it's a sincere statement, which is the right instinct. The writing team buried the pun inside a genuine expression of purpose, making it feel earned rather than forced. High quotability because it's concise and the wordplay is transparent.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: What's your greatest accomplishment?

dialogue.speaker: Swim team kid
dialogue.line: I came in fourth.

jokes.text: Wrong, your greatest accomplishment is happening in two hours when this bill becomes law.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks the youth swim team their greatest accomplishment; a kid says 'We came in fourth in the county swim meet.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately dismisses their actual athletic achievement and replaces it with the passage of her bill.
jokes.explanation: Solid character moment — Leslie's enthusiasm for civic process eclipsing all else is on-brand. A bit predictable in structure (straight man gives real answer, Leslie overrides it with her agenda) but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey swim team! Who's ready to make some waves and build community?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Anyone? Come on, we can do a chant! Let's go, let's go!

jokes.text: Porpoise call scene — Leslie does a porpoise call that the kids no longer do, then awkwardly says 'I'm not weird. Okay, everybody leave.'
jokes.setup: Leslie enthusiastically attempts a porpoise call, presumably a team ritual she knew from a prior involvement with the group.
jokes.punchline: The kids don't join in, leaving her alone mid-call. She immediately tries to save face with 'I'm not weird. Okay, everybody leave.'
jokes.explanation: A good cringe beat. The fact that she immediately tries to shut it down with 'everybody leave' after saying 'I'm not weird' is a nice self-aware touch that softens the cringe into affection. Rewatch bonus because the physical commitment she must have shown in the porpoise call is implied and funny on repeat viewing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? I was just making a porpoise call. It's a legitimate animal communication technique.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that sounded like you were choking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well maybe if everyone would just listen for one second instead of judging me, you'd hear the subtle cetacean inflection!

jokes.text: And writing Star Trek fan fiction does not count. Ha ha ha. I... finished it last week. What's going on?
jokes.setup: April asks Ben if he's busy, adding 'and writing Star Trek fan fiction does not count' as a preemptive exclusion.
jokes.punchline: Ben's laugh trails off as he realizes the accusation is accurate — he finished the fic last week.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is elegant: April preemptively disqualifies a specific activity, Ben laughs as if it's absurd — then his laugh dies as he confirms it's true. The deflating 'I... finished it last week' is perfectly timed and reveals character (Ben's nerdiness, April's perceptiveness). The pause implied by the ellipsis is crucial. One of the episode's stronger dialogue jokes.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Are you busy?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was just about to play some Catan.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Never mind, you're busy.

jokes.text: Dude, 30 years from now, when you're on your deathbed, what are you going to remember? Organizing files or taking a spontaneous road trip to surprise Leslie?
jokes.setup: Ben says he was going to get a jump on some work this weekend.
jokes.punchline: April — who is characteristically sullen and misanthropic — makes an uncharacteristically sincere and persuasive argument for spontaneity, using a deathbed hypothetical.
jokes.explanation: The joke is mostly that April is capable of sincere warmth and she's using it to manipulate Ben into a road trip. Decent character moment but the deathbed framing is a common comedic device and not especially original here.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Star Trek fan fiction is the lowest form of entertainment.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's... that's weird. Who would do that?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, not me. Definitely not me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was just... I have some stuff I need to go work on.

jokes.text: You get snacks. I'll bring music. We'll jam out to some sweet tunage. — Actually, no. I don't want to go any more. / Just kidding. See you in ten minutes. / Just kidding. We're not going. / Road trip! / So we're going? / Yes!
jokes.setup: The road trip plan is coming together enthusiastically.
jokes.punchline: April yanks the emotional rug out repeatedly — 'I don't want to go anymore' then 'just kidding' then 'just kidding, we're not going' then 'Road trip!' — torturing Ben with uncertainty as a form of play.
jokes.explanation: The escalating fake-outs are perfectly calibrated to April's character — she enjoys messing with people as a primary mode of affection. The beat lands because (a) we enjoy watching Ben suffer and (b) we know April actually wants to go. The triple reversal is one beat longer than expected, which is structurally smart.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't know if this road trip is a good idea. What if something goes wrong?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ben, you can't live your whole life worried about what might go wrong. You have to actually do things. Take risks. Live.

jokes.text: I'm excited to bond a little with April. She's like the little sister I never had. Because the little sister I do have is normal and not terrifying.
jokes.setup: Ben in a talking head, expressing excitement about the road trip with April.
jokes.punchline: He explains April is like the little sister he never had — then immediately undermines it by acknowledging his actual sister is normal and therefore unlike April.
jokes.explanation: Clean confessional joke with a well-constructed self-correction. Ben's straight-man awareness of April's terrifying quality, combined with his genuine warmth toward her, is character-specific. 'Normal and not terrifying' as the defining characteristic of a sibling is funny in its specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm so pumped for this road trip! We're going to have the best tunage playing the whole way.

jokes.text: Government is inefficient and should be dissolved. Please hold while I transfer you.
jokes.setup: A caller has tried to get a pothole fixed four times through proper channels. Andy sympathizes.
jokes.punchline: Andy's empathy with the caller leads him to openly agree the government should be dissolved — then immediately return to his government job function.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: the anarchist declaration ('should be dissolved') immediately followed by the bureaucratic continuation ('please hold while I transfer you') captures the fundamental absurdity of government self-critique from within government. Andy's complete lack of self-awareness about the contradiction is the key. 'Please hold' is the ideal punchline word — it's so mundane against the revolutionary sentiment. Justifies 8+ because it works on multiple levels: character comedy, political satire, and irony, all in 12 words.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're not going.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Just kidding, we're going.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh thank God.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Sike, we're not going.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: April!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm messing with you. We're definitely going.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're the worst.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, we're not.

jokes.text: How do I get I.T. here? / Call 311. / 311, how can I... Hello again, Diane.
jokes.setup: Andy gets a 311 call that's just static and asks Donna how to get I.T. support.
jokes.punchline: Donna tells him to call 311 — Andy calls 311, reaches himself, and immediately reaches the same caller stuck in the loop.
jokes.explanation: A nice bureaucratic loop gag. The fact that Andy calls his own line and immediately gets the same caller he was trying to help is a crisp structural payoff. The joke satirizes government inefficiency without being mean-spirited.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: April is nothing like my normal sister. My sister is responsible, organized, has her life together.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: April once spent an entire weekend rearranging her furniture in her apartment just to avoid going to brunch with me.

jokes.text: Donna, they switched my phone with 911. What do I do? / I don't know. Try to help. Now hush.
jokes.setup: Andy realizes his 311 phone has been switched with the actual 911 line.
jokes.punchline: Donna's advice is to 'try to help' and 'hush' — both of which are spectacularly inadequate responses to accidentally being the city's emergency line.
jokes.explanation: Donna's casual dismissal of what is technically an emergency situation is in perfect character. 'Now hush' is a wonderfully dismissive capper. The comedy comes from the gap between the stakes (people calling 911) and the response (Andy trying to help with zero training, Donna not caring).

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Hello, you've reached the Parks Department. How can I help you today?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, I'm sorry to hear that. Unfortunately, the government is a self-serving bureaucratic machine designed to waste your time and money, so there's really nothing we can do about it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Have a day.

jokes.text: It is heating up in this piece. / That sounds awful. / Good lord, it is hot. / Yes, mercy me. / Living in this town's like living in the devil's butt crack.
jokes.setup: Andy is now handling actual 911 calls, apparently connected to a caller in distress from the heat.
jokes.punchline: The caller describes living in Pawnee as 'living in the devil's butt crack' — an absurdly vivid and specific complaint that Andy receives with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'Living in the devil's butt crack' is a memorable and vivid piece of Pawnee self-description. It's quotable and fits the show's tradition of Pawnee citizens having extremely colorful opinions about their own town. Andy's 'that sounds awful' as a response to what is apparently a 911 emergency is also funny in its inadequacy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Donna, the 311 system is down. What do I do?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Call 311.

jokes.text: Almost out of gas. / I'll wait till we're on the highway.
jokes.setup: Ben notices they're almost out of gas.
jokes.punchline: April's plan to wait until they're on the highway to fill up defies basic logic — they'll run out before they get there.
jokes.explanation: A small joke setting up a later payoff (running out of gas). April's casual illogic is in character but the joke itself is functional rather than inspired. It earns its place as setup for later escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have everything a man needs in this office. A desk, a chair, a phone, some pencils, a notepad, a stapler, a tape dispenser, a trash can, a filing cabinet, a lamp, a calendar, a clock, some thumbtacks, a rubber band, a paper clip holder, a pen, a highlighter, some Post-it notes, a scissors, a ruler, a hole punch, a letter opener, some envelopes, a stamp, some paper, a binder, a folder, some index cards, a calculator, a three-hole punch, a label maker, a desk organizer, a desk pad, a desk calendar, a desk lamp, a desk fan, a desk plant, a desk photo frame, a desk drawer organizer, a rolling chair, a desk hutch, a lateral filing cabinet, a vertical filing cabinet, a credenza, a bookshelf, a coat rack, a door, a doorknob, a door hinge, a door frame, a wall, some drywall, some insulation, some plywood, some two-by-fours, a circular saw, a pneumatic nail gun, a reciprocating saw, a belt sander, a power drill, some concrete mix, some rebar, and a cement mixer.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, I think you got a little off track there.

jokes.text: My God, that is so interesting to me because I'm a map salesman.
jokes.setup: April tries to show Ben a cool alternate route she found on a map — a GPS vs. paper map debate.
jokes.punchline: A random passing stranger spontaneously interjects that he finds this interesting because he's a map salesman — completely unprompted and then presumably never seen again.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist non-sequitur that gets its laugh from total unexpectedness. Low character integration since it's a throwaway one-liner from a nobody, but the randomness is the point. Parks and Rec occasionally deploys these Pawnee-resident-as-comedic-prop jokes effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Now it's connected to emergency services

jokes.text: Why aren't we moving? / Because. Other cars. / Will you not do that? Please don't. / That's what you do when you... / Please don't do... Great, here comes a guy.
jokes.setup: They're stuck in traffic. April asks why they aren't moving; Ben gives an obvious answer and presumably gestures or honks.
jokes.punchline: Ben's exasperated back-and-forth as April apparently honks or does something obnoxious in traffic, culminating in 'Great, here comes a guy' — implying she's provoked a road rage incident.
jokes.explanation: A mostly visual gag that we can only partially reconstruct from transcript. 'Great, here comes a guy' is a funny understatement for a road rage confrontation. Rewatch bonus because what April actually does in traffic would be visible on screen and presumably escalates the comedy considerably.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: It is so hot out there, it's like the devil's armpit had a baby with the sun's butt.

jokes.text: It's because the two leading industries here are corn syrup and rubber nipples. It is a dentistry jackpot.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Jamm why he moved to Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Jamm's reason for moving to Pawnee: the town's terrible diet (corn syrup) and infant feeding products (rubber nipples) make it a perfect market for a dentist.
jokes.explanation: This is an excellent joke that uses worldbuilding (Pawnee's famously bad food culture) as character comedy (Jamm is a dentist who thinks entirely in business terms). 'Rubber nipples' as an industry alongside corn syrup is a genuinely funny pairing. 'It is a dentistry jackpot' is the perfect punchline — concise, mercenary, and character-specific. The joke reveals Jamm's cynical worldview while being genuinely clever about Pawnee's established lore.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh wow, a GPS route. How thrilling. I'm sure it's going to change my life in ways I never thought possible. Maybe it'll also make me a sandwich and teach me the meaning of existence.

jokes.text: Beautiful, Tom. Beautiful. Dynamite gums.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to ingratiate himself with Jamm to get into the Smokehouse.
jokes.punchline: Jamm compliments Tom's gums — a dentist obsessing over gums is perfectly in character and slightly gross.
jokes.explanation: 'Dynamite gums' is a funny phrase — the specificity of a dentist complimenting gums rather than teeth, plus the macho compliment register ('Dynamite'), gives it character comedy value.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why is traffic so bad today?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, cars are large metal boxes that move on wheels, and they need space between them to avoid colliding. When there are many cars on the road at once, each one takes up space, and they all have to move slower because of the increased density of vehicles. Also, some people don't know how to drive.

jokes.text: Well, D.D.S. doesn't stand for 'dumb, dumb, stupid.'
jokes.setup: Tom has expressed admiration for Jamm's dental market logic.
jokes.punchline: Jamm self-aggrandizes with a fake acronym expansion of his professional credentials — 'D.D.S. doesn't stand for dumb, dumb, stupid.'
jokes.explanation: A clean, efficient joke. The fake acronym expansion ('dumb, dumb, stupid') works because it's a weird, slightly childish insult construction — not 'dumb, dumb, idiot' or anything more polished. The awkwardness of the phrase is intentional character comedy. High quotability because it's portable out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I moved to Pawnee specifically to target industries that would ruin teeth.

jokes.text: Tom says he'll steal the D.D.S. joke — Jamm says 'All right. Cool.' then immediately pivots to 'Hey, so, we're still all good on Leslie's bill, right?' revealing he's been cozying up to Tom for political leverage.
jokes.setup: Tom and Jamm have been bonding; Tom expresses admiration and plans to steal the joke.
jokes.punchline: Jamm accepts the flattery and immediately pivots to asking about Leslie's bill vote — revealing the entire bonhomie was transactional.
jokes.explanation: A good structural beat that recontextualizes the preceding charm as calculation. More plot mechanics than pure joke but the pivot is abrupt enough to get a laugh from the whiplash.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I have a degree in dentistry.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Well, I have a degree in dentistry from a very reputable online university.

jokes.text: I have wanted this perm since middle school. I could not be more excited about this.
jokes.setup: Leslie is getting a perm, and we know Ann specifically told her not to.
jokes.punchline: Leslie is euphorically excited about the perm, which the audience knows is a terrible idea, especially given Ann's explicit warning.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the perm joke payoff later. Comedically functional but not remarkable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Check out my new personalized cigar cutter.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Oh, that's nice. Wait, is that... is that my name on there?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I had it engraved.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: So this is for me?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, it's for me. I just got your name engraved on it so you'd know how it feels when I use it.

jokes.text: Ann has told me repeatedly not to get a perm. But Ann's not here. So when the Ann's away, the mice get perms.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in the salon chair about to get the perm Ann explicitly forbade.
jokes.punchline: A riff on 'when the cat's away, the mice will play' — adapted to 'when the Ann's away, the mice get perms.' The awkward specificity of 'the Ann' makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The adaptation of the idiom works because of the specificity — 'the Ann' instead of 'the cat' is the right choice; keeping the definite article ('the mice') makes it feel like a real idiom rather than a slapped-together substitution. The joke is character-specific to Leslie and Ann's dynamic. High quotability — the phrase works completely out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm getting a perm because when the cat's away, the mice will play. And I am that mouse.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, that's not how that saying goes.

jokes.text: Councilman Jamm changed his vote. He's voting no on fun in the sun. / What? Why? He promised me. / He just said that he changed his mind. Then he told me some veneers could really make my smile pop.
jokes.setup: Tom reports the crisis: Jamm switched his vote.
jokes.punchline: Tom adds that Jamm segued into a sales pitch for veneers — Jamm cannot stop being a dentist even in political betrayal.
jokes.explanation: The veneer sales pitch as a non-sequitur following the vote betrayal is good Jamm character work. He's so defined by his dentistry that even political sabotage gets a product plug.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm postponing my perm. For politics.

jokes.text: The perm must wait, Autumn! The perm must wait.
jokes.setup: Leslie is mid-perm when a political crisis erupts and she needs to leave immediately.
jokes.punchline: 'The perm must wait, Autumn!' — Leslie addresses the stylist by name in a moment of dramatic crisis as if the perm is a geopolitical matter.
jokes.explanation: The comedic value comes from the absurd gravity with which Leslie treats both the political crisis and the perm. Addressing the stylist by name ('Autumn!') as if she were a field general is a great touch. 'The perm must wait' is highly quotable out of context. The repetition of the line adds to the gravitas parody.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: We don't have enough votes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if you spent less time playing video games and more time knocking on doors, we'd have enough votes!

jokes.text: The bill isn't going to pass? My parents said that you guys can't get anything done.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Tom are discussing the political crisis in front of the youth swim team.
jokes.punchline: A child flatly parrots his parents' anti-government cynicism directly to Leslie's face.
jokes.explanation: Kids voicing adult cynicism is a reliable comedic device. Works here because Leslie is trying desperately to show kids how great government is, making the child's criticism particularly deflating.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dammit, dammit, dammit, dammit, dammit!

jokes.text: Yeah, I know how to do math, Mason.
jokes.setup: A kid explains the vote math (3-2 against).
jokes.punchline: Leslie, clearly stressed, snaps at the child by name: 'Yeah, I know how to do math, Mason.'
jokes.explanation: The use of the kid's name 'Mason' makes this land — it's more specific and condescending than just snapping generically. Leslie being stress-snappy with a child she's trying to inspire is good irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How do I look?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You look... like you're in the middle of a process.

jokes.text: The bill is dead, the Porpoises are doomed, and democracy is over. My God.
jokes.setup: Tom has been told to stay positive. He pulls Leslie aside.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately catastrophizes to the maximum possible degree: from bill failure → Porpoises doomed → democracy is over. The 'My God' is a perfect cap.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from minor municipal bill to 'democracy is over' in two beats is well-constructed. 'My God' as a final beat is Tom performing crisis rather than experiencing it. Good character work showing Tom's flair for the dramatic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hark! The younglings doth demand I seek the counsel of the authorities before I may repair yon crater in the thoroughfare!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Verily, I shall not lay hammer to stone without the blessing of the crown!

jokes.text: I can't believe I decided to get a perm. Ann should have never let me do this.
jokes.setup: Tom has just declared democracy over.
jokes.punchline: Tom pivots immediately from world-historical crisis to lamenting his personal perm decision — and blames Ann for not stopping him.
jokes.explanation: The whiplash from 'democracy is over' to 'I can't believe I got a perm' is a nice comedic gear-shift that reveals Tom's true priority hierarchy. Blaming Ann for not stopping him is a good character detail — Tom deflects responsibility habitually.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why do you have so many movie soundtracks?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because music is the language of the soul, April. A great soundtrack doesn't just accompany a film—it elevates it. It transforms ordinary moments into something transcendent. John Williams didn't just compose for Star Wars; he composed the very essence of adventure itself.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're insane.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Passionate. There's a difference.

jokes.text: He's just trying to get something in return. This is a bargaining tool. / You know, this is why people hate the government.
jokes.setup: Tom correctly identifies Jamm's vote-flip as a negotiating tactic. Leslie is outraged.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, who works for the government and loves it deeply, says 'this is why people hate the government' — the ultimate irony for her character.
jokes.explanation: Good character irony — Leslie is the show's most ardent government booster, so her saying 'this is why people hate the government' is maximum cognitive dissonance for her. The joke is mild but character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What's on that mix?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, just some songs I like.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What's it called?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Uh... 'Ben's Sensitive Playlist.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: 'Cause just when we're about to do something really good, it all falls apart due to some stupid, selfish jerk butt.
jokes.setup: Leslie is venting about Jamm's political games.
jokes.punchline: 'Jerk butt' — Leslie's version of a curse word. Her inability to swear properly even in genuine outrage is a defining character trait.
jokes.explanation: Maximum character integration — 'jerk butt' is perfectly Leslie. She's genuinely upset, which makes the mild profanity substitute funnier. The escalating setup ('stupid, selfish jerk...') leads you to expect something stronger, making 'butt' a perfect letdown/punchline. High character integration score.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Before you say anything, I want you to know that I specifically requested this song.

jokes.text: Milton? He's, like, 150 years old. / Yeah. He's got grandkids, okay? And kids love to swim. And he'll give us his vote. He's an old person, and I'll talk to him really slowly. He won't even know what he's doing.
jokes.setup: Leslie proposes getting Councilman Milton's vote instead of bargaining with Jamm.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's plan to get Milton's vote involves talking very slowly and banking on his age-related confusion — a surprisingly dark strategy from the show's moral center, delivered with total matter-of-fact confidence.
jokes.explanation: Darkly funny because Leslie is supposed to be the ethical one. 'He won't even know what he's doing' is an admission of elder manipulation delivered without a hint of self-awareness. The contrast between Leslie's values and her pragmatic scheming when under pressure is a good character comedy vein.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: I'm not going to rush my lunch. I've been eating my lunch at exactly 12:47 p.m. for the past fourteen years. It takes me nine minutes to walk to the break room, seven minutes to arrange my food in a specific pattern on my plate, and then I eat for exactly twenty-three minutes while reading the same newspaper clipping about a local zoning dispute from 2003. If I deviate from this schedule by even one minute, it throws off my entire day and I have to start the whole fourteen-year cycle over again.

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Andy. I really like your dress. / I'm a princess. / I'm a mermaid. / I'm the director of Parks and Recreation. I'm here to fix that hole.
jokes.setup: Ron and Andy arrive to fix a pothole in what turns out to be a yard where children are playing.
jokes.punchline: Andy introduces himself to children roleplaying as royalty by announcing he's 'the director of Parks and Recreation' — matching their earnestness. Ron then flatly states they're there to fix the hole.
jokes.explanation: Works because Andy's title announcement matches the children's self-important roleplaying without him being in on the joke. Ron's flat 'I'm here to fix that hole' is the deadpan reset. Andy's warmth toward children is a consistent character trait that makes even mundane interactions charming.

jokes.text: Your highnesses, we do humbly request thine permission to befix doth holes yonder.
jokes.setup: The children say Ron and Andy must ask permission to enter their 'kingdom' to fix the pothole.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately launches into a sincere but grammatically mangled pseudo-medieval speech, inventing words like 'befix' and using 'doth' incorrectly.
jokes.explanation: 'Befix' is an invented word that is somehow perfect — it communicates exactly what Andy means while sounding appropriately medieval-ish. The entire sentence is grammatically wrong but semantically clear, which is a precise portrait of Andy's intelligence level and good intentions. Maximum character integration — this could only be Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, so I made this salad with all these different ingredients from different cultures, right? I called it the 'United Nations Salad' to celebrate diversity.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: That's racist.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, it's the opposite of racist. It's celebrating different cultures coming together.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: You're putting them all in a bowl together against their will. That's literally a melting pot, which is a racial concept.

jokes.text: Your tax dollars at work.
jokes.setup: Ron watches Andy chase children around the yard trying to tag them as part of their game.
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers 'Your tax dollars at work' directly to camera — a perfect libertarian-flavored editorial on government employees playing games instead of working.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum impact. Ron's anti-government philosophy makes this line perfectly his, but he's also technically participating in the taxpayer waste he's criticizing. The camera address is a mockumentary beat that lands as a knowing wink. Maximum economy. Rewatch bonus because Ron's deadpan delivery would be everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's just Andy wrestling with some kids he found.

jokes.text: 'Benji's Cool Times Summer Jamz Mix' discovery — Ben is embarrassed; April insists on hearing it.
jokes.setup: April is going through Ben's music and finds a CD labeled 'Benji's Cool Times Summer Jamz Mix.'
jokes.punchline: The title alone is comedically comprehensive — 'Benji' (childish nickname), 'Cool Times' (earnest self-assessment), 'Summer Jamz' (spelled with Z for extra nineties cred). Ben's escalating protests while April insists on playing it.
jokes.explanation: Every element of the CD title is funny and adds character information about Ben. 'Benji' tells us he's the kind of person who gave himself a cute nickname. 'Cool Times' is the self-delusion. 'Jamz' with a Z is generationally specific and embarrassing. April's eagerness to weaponize it against him is perfect. High character integration and rewatch bonus because the actual song played would make this funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: I have so many grandchildren, I've had to name three of them Brad. And two of them Jennifer. I can't keep track of which Brad is which.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's a lot of Brads.

jokes.text: Don't judge me.
jokes.setup: The embarrassing mix CD is playing and it's clearly something mortifying (a recognizable early 90s hip hop song).
jokes.punchline: Ben's defeated 'Don't judge me' — delivered not as a request but as a surrender.
jokes.explanation: A functional capper to the mix tape bit. 'Don't judge me' is a common phrase but earns its place here because the setup is strong enough to make the delivery land. Rewatch bonus since the actual song makes this scene significantly funnier on screen.

dialogue.line: Random guess about Tom's ethnicity

jokes.text: Councilman Milton was first elected as a city councilor in 1948, as a member of the Dixiecrat Party. Their platform? 'De-integrate Baseball.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is introducing Councilman Milton via talking head.
jokes.punchline: Milton's political history includes membership in the Dixiecrat Party with the specific platform of 'De-integrate Baseball' — a shockingly specific and real-seeming piece of racist political history delivered as casual exposition.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels. First, the Dixiecrat Party was a real thing, which grounds the absurdity in historical specificity. Second, 'De-integrate Baseball' as a platform is horrifying and funny because it's so specifically petty — not a grand civil rights opposition, but a particular objection to baseball integration. Third, it's delivered in Leslie's neutral exposition voice, as if this is simply interesting background information. The joke takes a dark historical reality and uses the specificity of the platform to generate comedy without trivializing the underlying history. Earns its 8+ because the concept is genuinely original and the execution is confident.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: His skin was like polished porcelain, cool to the touch yet radiating an inner warmth that defied his artificial nature. Data's golden eyes held the wisdom of a thousand starships, and when he spoke, it was as though the very fabric of the universe paused to listen to his melodious voice.

jokes.text: The secret is in the dressing. Try it. It's an aphrodisiac. / You too, my strange, foreign friend.
jokes.setup: Milton has been eating Caesar salad and invites Leslie and Tom to try it.
jokes.punchline: He describes the Caesar dressing as an aphrodisiac and also refers to Tom as 'my strange, foreign friend' — a casually offensive categorization from a man established as having a racist political history.
jokes.explanation: Milton's 'strange, foreign friend' directed at Tom (who is American) is consistent with his established Dixiecrat backstory — his worldview is hilariously antiquated. The aphrodisiac salad claim adds a layer of oblivious octogenarian confidence. Character integration is high because these jokes only work with this specific character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've read your fan fiction. It was very bad. I'm going to remember this.

jokes.text: I'm not eating racist salad.
jokes.setup: Milton has invited Tom to try the Caesar salad, having just called him a 'strange, foreign friend.'
jokes.punchline: Tom flatly refuses to eat 'racist salad' — transferring the racism of the man to his food.
jokes.explanation: Three words, one of the best jokes in the episode. 'Racist salad' is a perfectly absurd conflation — food cannot be racist, but Tom's logic is emotionally sound and character-specific. The joke acknowledges Milton's racism while giving Tom dignity and a witty deflection. Maximum economy: three words do everything. Highly quotable and generalizable. This is what a clean 8+ looks like — original concept, perfect economy, high character integration, earns the laugh through wit not shock.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Ron, would you be amenable to accompanying me to Food and Stuff this evening for provisions?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Diane, that's just asking if I want to go to the grocery store.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: I prefer to maintain a certain eloquence in my discourse.

jokes.text: The more we eat, the faster we talk. / Mmm. You can really taste the ignorance.
jokes.setup: Leslie wants Tom to eat the salad to accelerate Milton's eating so they can get to the vote conversation.
jokes.punchline: Tom eats it and delivers the verdict: 'You can really taste the ignorance' — a callback to the racist context, maintaining his protest while complying.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback to 'racist salad.' 'You can really taste the ignorance' extends the bit by having Tom describe the flavor of racism — which is absurd but internally consistent with his earlier logic. Extremely quotable. The callback structure adds value by building on the previous joke rather than just repeating it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: ♪ R-O-N and D-I-A-N-E, sittin' in a tree... ♪

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, how do you spell Diane? Is it D-I-A-N-E or D-I-A-N-A? No wait, that's a different name...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, ♪ R-O-N and D... some letters... E! ♪

jokes.text: It's pronounced 'anchovies.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just delivered 'you can really taste the ignorance' while eating the salad.
jokes.punchline: Milton misinterprets Tom's statement as a mispronunciation and corrects him: 'It's pronounced anchovies.' This suggests Milton either mishears 'ignorance' as 'anchovies' or chooses to interpret it that way.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. The structure is immaculate: Tom says 'ignorance,' Milton corrects 'anchovies.' The punchline works on three simultaneous levels: (1) phonetically, 'ignorance' and 'anchovies' don't sound alike, which makes the confusion funnier; (2) Milton is so old/oblivious that he genuinely mishears it; (3) OR Milton is so oblivious to his own ignorance that the word doesn't register as potentially referring to him. The salad context makes 'anchovies' a plausible misinterpretation, which is brilliant writing — the misdirection is built into the scene's physical reality. Maximum economy (five words). Rewatch bonus because you want to go back and listen to how Tom says 'ignorance' to understand the gag. This approaches the upper tier of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I have IBS, okay? Irritable Bowel Syndrome. It's a medical condition. I can't just hold it like you people.

jokes.text: Ron Swanson fixing a pothole himself — 'Yes, ma'am. Yes, I do.' when asked if he knows what he's doing.
jokes.setup: Diane asks if Ron, a government Parks employee with no Public Works credentials, knows what he's doing fixing her pothole.
jokes.punchline: Ron's absolute confidence — 'Yes, ma'am. Yes, I do.' — delivered with total certainty, because Ron genuinely does know how to do everything.
jokes.explanation: Ron's hyper-competent self-reliance is his defining trait, so his absolute confidence in fixing a pothole without credentials is perfectly in character. The double affirmation ('Yes, ma'am. Yes, I do.') conveys that even the question slightly offends him. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Jeremy. You need to learn to contain your bathroom issues like the rest of us.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: But I have a very sensitive digestive system.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then I suggest you see a doctor, not a city council woman.

jokes.text: And seven great-grandkids. Tim, Mary, Jack, uh, Tim, Marie, Tim, and Mary. / Don't forget about Tim. / Right, Tim. / How many is that? / You know, it's very hard to tell.
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions Milton has grandchildren to build rapport for the vote.
jokes.punchline: Milton lists seven great-grandkids with only three names between them (Tim, Mary, and Jack), repeating Tim and Mary multiple times. When Leslie asks how many that is, Milton concludes 'it's very hard to tell.'
jokes.explanation: The joke builds gradually and the payoff — 'it's very hard to tell' how many grandchildren you have — is perfect. The repetition of Tim is funny in itself, and Leslie's 'Don't forget about Tim' while trying to be helpful is a great detail showing her attempting to navigate this gracefully. 'It's very hard to tell' suggests Milton can't keep track of his own family, which is both sad and very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, come on, we need costumes for the party.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. I don't do costumes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But Ron, everyone's going to be dressed up!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I will be dressed up. In clothes. My clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, what if we both went as something cool? Like, what if we both became princesses?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Ron is given lemonade by Diane and they have a normal, pleasant interaction — a visual contrast to Andy in the background apparently playing with the children.
jokes.setup: Ron and Diane are having a polite, adult conversation about pothole repair.
jokes.punchline: Andy is presumably still playing with the children in the background, visible but unacknowledged — the contrast between Ron's stoic professionalism and Andy's childlike engagement.
jokes.explanation: Inferred visual gag. The contrast between Ron's dignity and Andy's background antics is a reliable comic device in this show. Rewatch bonus because background Andy is always worth catching.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: You remind me of a young George Wallace.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not sure how to take that.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: Oh, it's a compliment. He was very determined.

jokes.text: Lemonade? Please and thank you.
jokes.setup: Diane approaches Ron while he's working on the pothole.
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'Please and thank you' as an all-in-one response is a funny efficiency — he condenses both the acceptance and the gratitude into a single economical phrase.
jokes.explanation: Small but effective Ron moment. 'Please and thank you' as a combined preemptive phrase is economical and slightly formal in a way that's very Swanson. Also echoed later when Ron asks Diane to dinner ('Please and thank you'), making it a character verbal tic that becomes a callback.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: Leslie was very aggressive with me.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: She had this insatiable hunger for... for expansion, for growth, for meetings.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: I've never seen anything like it. It was like watching a beautiful, terrifying force of nature.

jokes.text: That's where I got these gloves. / Right?
jokes.setup: Diane mentions she got the lemonade from Food and Stuff (a Pawnee grocery store).
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he also shops at Food and Stuff — for work gloves. A tiny moment of unexpected common ground, delivered with Ron's characteristic lack of social decoration.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Ron's casual revelation that he shops for work gloves at a grocery store, and his 'Right?' — a rare moment of Ron seeking social confirmation. It's a small joke but perfectly Ron, suggesting he finds common ground with people through the most practical possible channels.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm concerned about your dental hygiene. You should really use this toothbrush.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Jamm, I appreciate the gesture, but my teeth are fine.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Tom, your teeth look like a row of tombstones at a neglected cemetery. I'm not trying to be mean, but if I had teeth like yours, I'd keep my mouth shut forever.

jokes.text: ♪ Ron and Diane / sitting in a tree / k-i-s-s-i-s-s-i-p-p-i.
jokes.setup: Ron and Diane are having a pleasant, mildly flirtatious interaction while fixing the pothole.
jokes.punchline: Andy sings a mangled version of 'sitting in a tree, K-I-S-S-I-N-G' — replacing the spelling with 'K-I-S-S-I-S-S-I-P-P-I' (Mississippi), a genuine mistake that accidentally creates a new word.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The concept is deceptively simple: Andy tries to tease Ron with a childhood song but mangles the spelling by conflating 'K-I-S-S-I-N-G' with 'Mississippi' — two things a child confuses because they share letters. The brilliance is that this error is EXACTLY the mistake Andy would make. It's not random — it's a specific, logical, character-revealing error. The result ('k-i-s-s-i-s-s-i-p-p-i') is funnier than the original song because it's longer, more absurd, and completely ruins the rhythm. The joke rewards attention because you have to decode what happened to appreciate it. Maximum character integration — only Andy would make this specific mistake. Extremely quotable. Earns a clear 8+ because the comedic concept is genuinely original and the character integration is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I will not compromise with Jamm on this. And I will not compromise with Big Dental either. Those corporate tooth tyrants have had it too good for too long.

jokes.text: Jamm wants Leslie's office because of the private bathroom — 'I don't mean to brag, but I've got Irritable Bowel Syndrome.'
jokes.setup: Jamm has torpedoed Leslie's bill not for policy reasons but because he wants her office with the private bathroom.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't mean to brag, but I've got Irritable Bowel Syndrome.' Jamm treats a medical condition as a status symbol.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the opening scene (Jamm using Leslie's bathroom) pays off spectacularly. 'I don't mean to brag' before announcing a bowel disorder is a perfect inversion of the phrase's expected use. Treating IBS as a point of pride is genuinely original and maximally Jamm. The phrase also works as a callback to his opening 'drop my liquids / take my solids' comment, completing the character portrait. Earns 8+ because the inversion of 'I don't mean to brag' is a sharp structural choice and the character integration is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: You look like a princess had a stroke.

jokes.text: He shoots down a very helpful bill 'cause he doesn't get to poop wherever he wants? / No, I'm gonna get Councilman Milton, and you can put your butt back in your pants, sir.
jokes.setup: Leslie is outraged that Jamm's obstruction is purely bathroom-related.
jokes.punchline: 'Put your butt back in your pants, sir' — another Leslie near-profanity that is simultaneously dignified (the 'sir') and ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Another excellent Leslie near-profanity. 'Put your butt back in your pants, sir' is absurdly formal for what it's saying. The addition of 'sir' is the key — Leslie's politeness instinct kicks in even during an insult. Running character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Finally getting traffic moving

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Immediately hitting another obstacle

jokes.text: Andy, come help me tamp this down. / For the last time, Ron, it's Princess Rainbow Sparkle.
jokes.setup: Ron calls for Andy's help with the pothole work.
jokes.punchline: 'For the last time, Ron, it's Princess Rainbow Sparkle.' Andy has been absorbed into the children's game and has taken on a princess persona — and this has apparently been an ongoing correction.
jokes.explanation: 'For the last time' implies Andy has been insisting on being called Princess Rainbow Sparkle through multiple exchanges we didn't see — the 'for the last time' construction retroactively builds a longer bit. 'Princess Rainbow Sparkle' as Andy's chosen identity is perfect. The contrast with Ron's stoic pothole work is maximum. High character integration — Andy's childlike joy in roleplay is a core trait.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I finally got the bathroom I wanted. It took some work, but I made it happen.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's great, Jeremy. How did you manage that?

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Well, let's just say I had to grease some wheels, if you know what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: ...What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I mean I literally gave money to the contractor. To grease the wheels of bureaucracy. With actual money. I paid him.

jokes.text: I think it would really make Diane happy. / Why would that matter? / Shut up.
jokes.setup: Andy suggests Ron dress as a princess to make Diane happy, implying he's noticed Ron's interest in her.
jokes.punchline: Ron asks 'Why would that matter?' then immediately, without waiting for an answer: 'Shut up.' — a perfect self-correction that reveals he knows exactly why it matters.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is beautiful: Ron asks a question ('why would that matter?') and immediately answers his own question by shutting down the conversation before the answer can come ('shut up') — because the answer would require him to admit he has feelings for Diane. The speed of the self-correction is the joke. Maximum character integration — Ron's emotional suppression expressed through rapid subject-change is quintessentially him. Earns its 8+ because the structure is elegant and the self-censorship does character work efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I've given birth in positions that would make a yogi uncomfortable. I did it in a squat, I did it on all fours, I did it while doing the splits. My doctor said, 'Donna, I've never seen anything like this.' I said, 'Well, get used to it, because I'm about to do it again.'

jokes.text: You remind me of a young, beautiful Strom Thurmond. / Yes, I've been saying that for years.
jokes.setup: Milton is complimenting Leslie during their conversation.
jokes.punchline: The 'compliment' he gives is being compared to Strom Thurmond — a notoriously segregationist politician. Leslie's response ('Yes, I've been saying that for years') is the perfect absurdist beat: she enthusiastically accepts a comparison that should horrify her.
jokes.explanation: Works as character comedy for both characters: Milton's frame of reference is deeply problematic historical figures, and Leslie's desperation for the vote makes her accept the comparison without processing its content. The 'young, beautiful' modifier before Strom Thurmond is an additional absurdity layer. Leslie's response is the punchline — 'I've been saying that for years' implies she considers this a legitimate self-comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about. I have no feelings for Diane. I barely know her. And even if I did, which I don't, it wouldn't matter because I'm not capable of human emotion.

jokes.text: Would you please come help me tamp this down? It's a job that requires two men. Or does it require two princesses?
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to get Andy back to work.
jokes.punchline: Ron's self-correction — 'Or does it require two princesses?' — is an unexpected concession to the game from the most stoic man alive.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson using princess roleplay as a management technique is intrinsically very funny. The progression from 'two men' to 'or does it require two princesses' shows Ron making a pragmatic concession — he'll work within Andy's framework if it gets the job done. The idea of Ron as a princess doing pothole work is excellent visual comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So about this weekend, I was thinking we could finally go to that bed and breakfast upstate.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Really? That sounds amazing.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, or we could go skydiving. Or visit my parents. Or literally anything else I haven't told you about yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: April, what's going on?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm just getting you back for all those times you changed our plans last minute without telling me. Remember? The camping trip? The concert? Your budget committee meetings that suddenly became more important than literally everything?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That was... okay, fair point.

jokes.text: There's a lot of salad dressing on your hand. Shall we kiss? / No. No! / My God, are you okay? Please be okay. Please, still be able to vote.
jokes.setup: Milton seemingly has a health event (presumably grabbing his chest or some dramatic movement) after suggesting they kiss.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's concern is split between genuine human worry ('please be okay') and immediately selfish political calculation ('please, still be able to vote'). The second concern arriving so quickly after the first is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of genuine human concern and naked political calculation in rapid succession is a solid joke about how politicians think. Leslie's self-awareness about the ugly thought but inability to suppress it is character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh thank God. For a second there I thought you meant something completely different.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What? No. I literally fixed the pothole on Maple Street.

jokes.text: We can kiss if you want to. / With tongue? / Hey! No.
jokes.setup: Milton has recovered and Leslie offers to kiss him (presumably on the cheek as a platonic gesture of goodwill).
jokes.punchline: 'With tongue?' — Milton's elderly lechery is maximally uncomfortable, and Leslie's 'Hey! No.' is the perfect non-defensive response.
jokes.explanation: The economy is high — 'with tongue?' does a lot of comedic work in two words. Milton's lechery is played as oblivious rather than malicious, which keeps it in the cringe-comedy zone. Slightly predictable structure (elderly character makes inappropriate suggestion) but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Ron, I think you're a good man. I'd like to take you to dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I... yes. I would like that very much.

jokes.text: She tried to kiss me. / She was insatiable.
jokes.setup: In a probable talking head, Milton recounts the encounter with Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Milton completely rewrites the interaction — he was the one who asked for the kiss — and describes Leslie as 'insatiable.' His self-mythology is total.
jokes.explanation: 'She was insatiable' as Milton's confessional reading of Leslie refusing him is a great joke about how his self-image works. The inversion is clean and the word 'insatiable' is a perfect choice — it's the word of a man who considers himself irresistible.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You have... very straight teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: For a woman.

jokes.text: Complimentary toothbrush? / You're missing the backs of your upper canines. / Sloppy technique. / Excuse me? / I have excellent toothbrush technique.
jokes.setup: Jamm runs into Leslie and offers a complimentary toothbrush — he's fundamentally a dentist at all times.
jokes.punchline: Jamm immediately critiques Leslie's brushing technique ('sloppy technique') and Leslie's outrage is about her toothbrush form, not the political situation.
jokes.explanation: Consistent Jamm character work — he literally cannot stop being a dentist. The absurdity of a political confrontation turning into a toothbrush technique critique is good. Leslie's indignation about her toothbrush technique rather than his political betrayal is a nice misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Leslie, I have to admit, your compromise is actually quite—

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: AHHHHHHH!

jokes.text: Just give him what he wants. Take the easy way out. I always do. It's so easy.
jokes.setup: Leslie is refusing to negotiate with Jamm. Tom is urging her to capitulate.
jokes.punchline: Tom's argument for taking the easy way out culminates in him openly admitting he 'always' takes the easy way out — not as self-criticism but as a sincere endorsement of the strategy.
jokes.explanation: Tom's cheerful self-awareness about his own moral laziness is consistently funny. 'It's so easy' as the final persuasive argument is perfect Tom — he's not ashamed, he's genuinely recommending it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no, no, no! My hair! Do you know how long it took me to get my hair like this? I followed a YouTube tutorial for forty-five minutes!

jokes.text: I do not negotiate with dentists.
jokes.setup: Tom urges Leslie to give Jamm what he wants.
jokes.punchline: Leslie paraphrases 'I do not negotiate with terrorists' — substituting 'dentists' for 'terrorists,' delivered with identical conviction.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable and clean jokes. The phrase 'I do not negotiate with terrorists' is culturally loaded with geopolitical gravity; substituting 'dentists' deflates it perfectly while also making contextual sense (Jamm is a dentist). The joke earns its 8+ through economy (six words), the specificity of the substitution (dentists vs. some random profession), and the character integration (Leslie's conviction makes it land). Would work as a standalone quote with no context.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Welcome to Tom's Cigar Club. As you can see, I have a chair here that's named after me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's called the Tom Haverford Relaxation Station.

jokes.text: I'm trying to tell everybody that the government is great, and I think it stinks. I hate it. I hate the government. / You don't mean that. / You're right, I don't. I take it back. Why did I say that, Tom? God, you know me so well.
jokes.setup: Leslie is having a crisis of faith in government under political pressure.
jokes.punchline: Leslie says she hates the government — the single most out-of-character statement possible — then immediately retracts it when Tom points this out. 'God, you know me so well' as the capper implies Tom's 'you don't mean that' was profound insight.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of how quickly Leslie corrects herself and how much emotional weight she gives to Tom's minimal input ('you don't mean that'). 'God, you know me so well' is funny because Tom did essentially nothing — he just pointed out the obvious. Leslie's genuine gratitude for being redirected back to herself is touching and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no strong feelings one way or the other.

jokes.text: I came here to fix a pothole, not be mocked. / I'm sorry, it's just... your face is ridiculous.
jokes.setup: Ron has apparently been dressed as a princess (per Andy's earlier suggestion) and finds Diane laughing at him.
jokes.punchline: Diane apologizes but can't help herself: 'It's just... your face is ridiculous.' Ron Swanson in full princess regalia, trying to maintain dignity, is the visual joke.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the princess thread. Ron Swanson — the show's most masculinity-committed character — wearing princess accessories while trying to maintain his stoic dignity is a classic Parks visual. 'Your face is ridiculous' is a good punchline because it's affectionate mockery. Rewatch bonus because Ron's princess look would be the main event visually.

jokes.text: I came here to fix a pothole, not be mocked. I'm sorry, it's just... your face is ridiculous.
jokes.setup: Ron, now apparently in princess attire, is being laughed at by Diane.
jokes.punchline: Diane's apology and 'your face is ridiculous' implies Ron is wearing princess makeup/costume — an extraordinary visual for Nick Offerman's face.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the princess storyline — Diane sees Ron in princess getup and cannot suppress laughter. 'Your face is ridiculous' directed at Nick Offerman/Ron Swanson in princess makeup is a strong visual joke with high rewatch appeal. The scene also establishes romantic chemistry through shared absurdity.

jokes.text: The presidential motorcade finally moves — then Ben and April run out of gas immediately.
jokes.setup: Ben and April have been stuck for ages behind a presidential motorcade. It finally moves.
jokes.punchline: The moment the road opens, they run out of gas — the exact fate April's 'wait till we're on the highway' plan guaranteed.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured callback that pays off the earlier gas joke. The timing is perfect — the bureaucratic delay (motorcade) was replaced immediately by April's self-created delay (no gas). The escalation of bad luck is satisfying structurally.

jokes.text: Councilman, I move that the bill be read in its entirety. / Ms. Beavers? / Fine.
jokes.setup: Leslie is stalling at the council meeting while she works on getting Jamm's vote.
jokes.punchline: Leslie moves to read the entire bill aloud — a classic parliamentary stalling tactic — and even the other councilors see through it immediately ('Buying time, I see. What's up?').
jokes.explanation: A decent situational joke — the stall is transparent to everyone. Councilwoman Beavers's 'fine' implies resigned familiarity with Leslie's shenanigans. Functional plot-comedy beat.

jokes.text: You can have my office. / Okay, why don't you sweeten the pot? / You can have my parking space. / And? / And I will get Invisaligns from you. / And? / And, that is enough. And shut up. And I hate you.
jokes.setup: Leslie is negotiating with Jamm for his vote.
jokes.punchline: Each concession is met with 'And?' — escalating until Leslie's final offer ends with 'And shut up. And I hate you' — a complete collapse of negotiating dignity.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure works because each 'And?' extends the negotiation and raises the stakes. The pivot from formal concessions ('Invisaligns') to 'And shut up. And I hate you' is a perfect tonal collapse. The 'And' construction is maintained even in the insults, which is a nice formal touch. Leslie's rage barely contained by negotiating language is character-specific.

jokes.text: Can't wait to drop my kids at the pool. / By 'kids,' I mean turds. / I get it.
jokes.setup: The deal is sealed. Jamm celebrates getting the bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Jamm uses the phrase 'drop the kids at the pool' (already a euphemism for defecating) then immediately explains it ('by kids I mean turds') — defeating the purpose of the euphemism while Leslie deadpans 'I get it.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: (1) 'Drop the kids at the pool' is already a known idiom, so Jamm using it is slightly funny; (2) his immediate explanation ('by kids I mean turds') destroys the euphemism — which is the point, because Jamm has no filter; (3) Leslie's 'I get it' is the perfectly withered response of someone who did not need that clarified. The callback to Jamm's bathroom fixation from the episode's opening is satisfying. High character integration because Jamm's complete absence of social grace is total.

jokes.text: Then Ana asks Grey to punish her. Donna, please, can you keep it down? / Or at least research how to deliver a baby that's coming out face up. / Lay the mother on her side and try to move the baby in a corkscrew fashion.
jokes.setup: Donna is apparently reading Fifty Shades of Grey aloud at the 311 desk. Andy asks her to keep it down.
jokes.punchline: Andy's correction is not about the content of what she's reading but about the noise — except what she's also apparently handling is an actual childbirth 911 call, which she has factual information about from... unclear sources.
jokes.explanation: A good multi-layered joke: Donna reading Fifty Shades is funny on its own; the pivot to midwifery instruction ('lay the mother on her side and try to move the baby in a corkscrew fashion') delivered in the same register is absurdly funny. The 'corkscrew fashion' phrasing is specific enough to be genuinely funny. Donna's competent delivery of medical information despite her job being neither medical nor emergency services is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: 'A,' I don't recall inviting you in here, and 'B,' I did not like her. Her life is messy. / Ron, messy is fun, okay? My whole life is a giant mess and I love it. I mean, look at my hair. I have gum in my hair.
jokes.setup: Andy tells Ron that Diane likes him and he likes her.
jokes.punchline: Andy's argument for pursuing Diane includes 'look at my hair, I have gum in my hair' — presented as evidence that messiness is charming rather than a problem.
jokes.explanation: Andy using gum in his hair as a positive advertisement for messiness is perfectly Andy. He's giving sincere relationship advice while simultaneously being a walking counterexample. The logic is internally coherent from Andy's perspective, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Diane is awesome and she likes you. And you like her. I can tell. 'A,' I don't recall inviting you in here, and 'B,' I did not like her. She's not my type. Her life is messy. Ron, messy is fun, okay? My whole life is a giant mess and I love it. I mean, look at my hair. I have gum in my hair.
jokes.setup: Andy has observed Ron's interaction with Diane and offers unsolicited romantic advice.
jokes.punchline: Andy's argument that Ron should embrace messy: 'My whole life is a giant mess and I love it. Look at my hair. I have gum in my hair.' — Andy's gum-in-hair evidence is both absurd and completely Andy.
jokes.explanation: Andy as relationship philosopher is gold. The escalation from life advice to hair advice to 'I have gum in my hair' as proof is a perfect Andy Dwyer move — he genuinely believes this is persuasive. Ron's 'A' and 'B' structure for deflecting shows his contempt even in conversation structure. Deep character integration for both.

jokes.text: That was a great road trip. / We made it 40 feet. / Yeah, well, at least it took a million hours, and it was 180 degrees, and we starved to death. / So fun.
jokes.setup: The road trip has ended in disaster — stranded on the highway, out of gas, having barely moved.
jokes.punchline: April sarcastically enumerates their failures ('a million hours,' '180 degrees,' 'starved to death') while Ben deadpans 'So fun.' — matching her irony with his own.
jokes.explanation: A good capper for the road trip subplot. The hyperbolic specificity ('a million hours,' '180 degrees') combined with 'starved to death' is April-consistent. Ben's 'So fun.' lands because he's now adopted her ironic register. The two characters meeting in shared irony is a nice relationship beat.

jokes.text: Yeah, you know what? All right, I'm in. You know, we might be able to sneak out early. You get snacks. I'll bring music. We'll jam out to some sweet tunage.
jokes.setup: Ben enthusiastically agrees to the road trip.
jokes.punchline: 'Sweet tunage' — Ben's attempt at cool road trip vernacular sounds profoundly uncool, consistent with 'Benji's Cool Times Summer Jamz Mix.'
jokes.explanation: Small character beat — 'sweet tunage' is the kind of dated slang that perfectly characterizes Ben as someone who peaked culturally in 1995. Works as setup for the Summer Jamz reveal.

jokes.text: Hey, how about next weekend we fly to Pawnee? Tickets are on me. / Really? That would be awesome. Definitely. / Nah, never mind. I don't feel like it. / What? My God. / See how it feels?
jokes.setup: Stranded on the road, April suggests they fly to Pawnee next weekend and offers to pay.
jokes.punchline: Ben gets genuinely excited; April immediately withdraws the offer ('Nah, never mind') as payback for the road trip reversal she pulled earlier. 'See how it feels?'
jokes.explanation: A perfect structural callback to the opening road trip fake-outs. The irony is that April spent this whole trip tormenting Ben with fake commitments, so she turns it around on him now that they're stranded and he's desperate. 'See how it feels?' is the ideal capper — April's mischief is always affectionate underneath, and this confirms she's been paying attention. The callback adds value by completing the arc.
